journal: JOURNAL OF THE ACOUSTICAL SOCIETY OF AMERICA
title: Modeling subjective evaluation of soundscape quality in urban open spaces: An artificial neural network approach
country: Germany; Greece; Italy; Switzerland; United Kingdom; China
setting: square (19 urban open spaces in 9 cities incl. squares, gardens, a street, a seashore and a park - e.g. Kassel Bahnhofsplatz, Athens Seashore, Sheffield Peace Gardens and Barkers Pool, Cambridge All Saint's Garden and Silver Street, Beijing Xi Dan Square, Shanghai Xu Jia Hui Park; located in city centres (7), residential areas (5), tourist spots (5) and near railway stations (2), Table I)
design: survey (large-scale on-site questionnaire interviews with concurrent multi-sensor physical measurements; site-level Pearson/Spearman correlations, t-tests and chi-square screening of physical, behavioural, social/demographic and psychological factors, followed by artificial neural network models and an ordinal logistic regression comparison)
sample_n: over 9000 interviewees in Europe and over 800 in China (section II.A); 62-1041 per site (Table I); acoustic comfort evaluation only at 7 sites (2 Sheffield, 5 China)
exposure: Reverse: user behavioural factors recorded at interview (B1 wearing earphones, B2 reading or writing, B3 watching somewhere, B4 movement status sitting/standing/playing with kids/sporting, B5 frequency of coming to the site 1 first time-5 every day, B6 reason for coming, B7 grouping none/1/more than 1 companion; Table II) as predictors of soundscape evaluation. Acoustic context: SPL (dBA, 1-min measurement) plus air temperature, wind speed, humidity and luminance measured with a multi-sensor station immediately before or after each interview; CadnaA-calculated SPL used for prediction maps (section IV)
behaviour_measure: Binary items for wearing earphones, reading/writing and watching somewhere; movement status (sitting, standing, playing with kids, sporting); frequency of coming to the site (5-point, first time to every day); reason for coming (equipment/services, children playing and social meetings, business/meeting/break, social events, passing by); grouping (alone, with 1 person, with more than 1 person) (Table II)
measurement_method: self-report (on-site face-to-face questionnaire interviews; recording mode for observable items B1-B4 not specified in this paper)
key_finding: Behavioural factors had limited, site-specific associations with the subjective sound level evaluation: watching somewhere (7/19 sites), reason for coming (7/16) and frequency of coming (5/19) were significant in at least 5 sites, whereas wearing earphones (0/4), reading/writing (2/19), movement status (2/19) and grouping (4/19) rarely were, and correlation signs varied across sites (e.g. frequency of coming r = -0.11 to 0.15). For acoustic comfort (7 sites) behavioural factors had limited importance, although grouping and movement status were retained as ANN inputs in some models.
effect_stats: Table III (sound level evaluation; Pearson/Spearman r for 3+ scale factors, two-tailed t-test mean differences for 2-scale factors, Pearson chi-square significance level for B6; * p<0.05, ** p<0.01; minus signs recovered from the source PDF because the text extraction dropped them): B5 frequency of coming significant at site 4 -0.10**, site 5 -0.11**, site 6 0.10**, site 7 0.15**, site 9 -0.07* (5/19, 26.3%); B7 grouping site 4 0.12**, site 8 0.10*, site 10 -0.09**, site 14 0.10* (4/19); B4 movement status site 2 -0.10*, site 8 -0.12** (2/19); B3 watching site 3 0.13*, 4 0.30**, 5 -0.31**, 7 -0.18*, 11 0.20*, 12 0.48**, 14 -0.49** (7/19); B2 reading/writing site 6 0.26*, site 14 0.46** (2/19); B6 reason for coming chi-square site 2 0.01*, 4 0.00**, 6 0.01**, 7 0.02*, 8 0.04*, 11 0.00**, 12 0.01** (7/16); B1 earphones 0/4. Acoustic comfort: behavioural factors described only as having limited importance, no statistics (section II.D). ANN inputs including behavioural factors, e.g. Peace Gardens acoustic comfort model with B7: test coefficient 0.79, RMSE 0.103 (Table VIII)

title: Spatial-temporal change analysis of plant soundscapes and their design methods
setting: park (Jinan Forest Park, Jinan - urban park of 69.5 hm2 with 60.1 hm2 green area at the foot of Kuangshan Mountain; 14 plant-space observation points S1-S14 classified as open, semi-open, closed or vertical space, Table 1)
design: survey (on-site LAeq and frequency measurements + researcher soundwalks rating sound-element clarity + interviews with passers-by; descriptive statistics, ANOVA and Spearman correlation)
sample_n: 1260 interviewees (convenience sampling of passers-by at each observation point, 5 females and 5 males in each of 3 age groups, over 3 days; section 2.2) (acoustic unit: 14 observation points measured in April, July, October 2014 and January 2015)
exposure: Reverse: visitor characteristics including self-reported visitation frequency (with age, gender and satisfaction with the park) related to preference ratings (5-point, 1 very dislike-5 very like) for 12 sound elements (bird chirping, frog and insect chirping, leaves rustling, brook babbling, artistic conception of sculpture, talking, children frolicking, singing and dancing, peddling, broadcast, traffic noise, constructing). Acoustic context: LAeq and octave-band levels measured with an AWA 6228-3 analyser in triplicate every 3 h from 6:00 to 18:00 for 3 days per season; soundwalk clarity ratings (-1 to 1) by 3 researchers
behaviour_measure: Self-reported visitation frequency to the park collected in the interview (response categories not reported)
measurement_method: self-report (face-to-face interviews with passers-by, about 6 min each)
key_finding: Visitation frequency was positively correlated with preference for nature sounds (bird chirping, leaves rustling, brook babbling) and negatively with preference for children frolicking; age showed a similar pattern, while gender and park satisfaction were not correlated with sound preference. The authors also attributed the highest LAeq at entrance/square points and the 9:00 LAeq peak at S2 and S11 to human activities such as dancing, but visitor activity was not measured.
effect_stats: Table 3 Spearman correlation of visitation frequency with preference: V1 bird chirping 0.263*, V2 frog and insect chirping 0.110, V3 leaves rustling in the wind 0.300**, V4 brook babbling 0.278*, V5 artistic conception of sculpture 0.017, V6 talking -0.060, V7 children frolicking -0.276*, V8 singing and dancing -0.045, V9 peddling -0.096, V10 broadcast 0.136, V11 traffic noise -0.179, V12 constructing -0.071 (n used for the correlations NR); LAeq differed across observation points and seasons, ANOVA F = 17.092, P < 0.001 (section 3.1, df NR)
